quote: produced an **82% reduction in inpatient suicide rate** (from 2.64 to 0.87 per 100,000 admissions, P < .001), sustained over 7 years.
problem: The headline percentage contradicts its own parenthetical: 2.64 to 0.87 per 100,000 is a 67% reduction, and 2.64/0.87 are the actual Watts 2012 figures. The page's flagship suicide-prevention number is inflated by 15 points, and the summary-table row ('82% reduction in inpatient suicide') repeats it, so learners will quote 82% on rounds and in write-ups.
replacement: produced a **67% reduction in inpatient suicide rate** (from 2.64 to 0.87 per 100,000 admissions, P < .001), sustained over 7 years.
basis: Watts BV et al., Arch Gen Psychiatry 2012 (rate fell from 2.64 to 0.87 per 100,000 admissions after MHEOCC implementation; (2.64-0.87)/2.64 = 67%); Watts 2017 Psychiatr Serv sustained-effect follow-up. The internal arithmetic is decisive regardless of source recall.

quote: environmental safety checklists cut inpatient suicide 82%
problem: The overlay TL;DR — the stripped-of-context card a rushed learner reads — repeats the inflated 82% figure; the page's own rates (2.64 to 0.87 per 100,000) work out to 67%. The key-points card ('produced an 82% reduction in the inpatient suicide rate') carries the same error, and the same TL;DR sentence also carries the '60%' odds-as-risk gloss (MS3V11-F006) and the unverified OR 0.18 (MS3V11-F004).
replacement: environmental safety checklists cut inpatient suicide 67%
basis: Watts BV et al., Arch Gen Psychiatry 2012: 2.64 to 0.87 per 100,000 admissions = 67% reduction.

quote: MIND-USA and AID-ICU both showed no benefit for antipsychotics vs. placebo on days alive without delirium or coma
problem: Days alive without delirium or coma was MIND-USA's primary endpoint only; AID-ICU's primary endpoint was days alive and out of the hospital at 90 days. The rationale — the text a learner memorizes after answering — mis-summarizes a landmark trial; the page prose two sections down states it correctly ('no significant difference in the primary outcome'), so the overlay and prose disagree.
replacement: MIND-USA showed no benefit for antipsychotics vs. placebo on days alive without delirium or coma, and AID-ICU showed none on days alive and out of the hospital at 90 days
basis: Girard et al., NEJM 2018 (MIND-USA primary outcome: days alive without delirium or coma); Andersen-Ranberg et al., NEJM 2022 (AID-ICU primary outcome: days alive and out of the hospital at 90 days).

quote: found FPE was the most efficacious for relapse prevention in schizophrenia at 12 months: OR 0.18 (95% CI 0.12–0.27), with only 10% relapsing vs. 37% with treatment as usual
problem: OR 0.18 (an ~80% odds reduction) is far stronger than the canonical family-intervention estimate this same volume teaches in the Therapy Reading Room (Pharoah Cochrane RR 0.55, NNT 7), and I cannot specifically recall Rodolico 2022 reporting 0.18 for family psychoeducation vs TAU — this reads like a possible mis-extraction (e.g., of a single-model credible-interval or a different comparison). It is also the TL;DR headline ('family psychoeducation cuts 12-month relapse (OR 0.18)') and a summary-table row, so if wrong it propagates.
replacement: found family psychoeducation was the most efficacious model for relapse prevention in schizophrenia at 12 months (Rodolico et al., Lancet Psychiatry 2022)
basis: Would be settled by the results table of Rodolico et al., Lancet Psychiatry 2022;9(3):211-221 (family psychoeducation vs TAU relapse OR and absolute relapse proportions). Pharoah et al. Cochrane 2010 (RR 0.55, NNT 7) is the benchmark the number must be reconciled against before re-adding it.

quote: | Delirium prevention | Multicomponent non-pharmacological | 53% reduction in incident delirium | Meta-analysis of 14 studies |
problem: This row typifies the page-wide pattern: ~13 summary-table rows and roughly two dozen prose statistics pair an effect size with a study design ('Meta-analysis of 14 studies', 'RCT (n=200)', 'Cochrane review (33 RCTs)') but no study identity, so a learner cannot get from any number to a paper even though the page ends in a full DOI bibliography — and the evidence-annotation gate cannot catch a wrong one because it only verifies claims somebody annotated. Residual chat artifacts ('Would you like to explore any of these domains in greater depth…', two dangling 'Figure 2 …' captions) show the page shipped as unedited generated output, which is exactly the provenance in which numbers like the 82% error (MS3V11-F001) survive.
replacement: | Delirium prevention | Multicomponent non-pharmacological | 53% reduction in incident delirium | Hshieh 2015 meta-analysis of 14 studies (JAMA Intern Med) |
basis: This row's source is identifiable (Hshieh et al., JAMA Intern Med 2015: 14 HELP-type studies, OR 0.47, 95% CI 0.38–0.58 — the number itself is correct); every other table row and design-only prose statistic needs the same author-year attribution. Site policy already requires claim-level traceability (evidence_annotations sourceSpan gate).

quote: produced a **60% reduction in post-discharge suicide attempts** (OR 0.40, 95% CI 0.20–0.80; NNT = 7)
problem: OR 0.40 is a 60% reduction in the odds of an attempt, not in attempts; with the outcome common enough to give NNT = 7, the implied relative risk reduction is roughly 50%, so the sentence overstates the flagship psychotherapy result. The TL;DR ('reduces post-discharge attempts 60% (NNT 7)') and the summary-table row ('60% reduction in attempts (NNT=7)') repeat the gloss, and learners will quote it to families as '60% fewer attempts'.
replacement: produced a **60% reduction in the odds of a post-discharge suicide attempt** (OR 0.40, 95% CI 0.20–0.80; NNT = 7)
basis: Odds ratios only approximate risk ratios when the outcome is rare; an NNT of 7 means it is not rare here (baseline risk ~25–30%, at which OR 0.40 corresponds to RR ~0.5). Diefenbach et al., JAMA Psychiatry 2024 reported the effect as an odds ratio.

quote: ties directly to §11's finding that pre-discharge 7-day follow-up is associated with lower suicide risk (HR ~0.82)
problem: §11 contains no HR at all — it states the association qualitatively — so this cross-reference invents a provenance for a number that appears nowhere else on the page and has no source; the only quantified 7-day-follow-up suicide estimate the page gives is RR 0.44 (in youth, §1). A learner who tries to trace HR 0.82 hits a dead end, and the false internal citation teaches that the page's cross-references can't be trusted.
replacement: ties directly to §11's finding that follow-up within 7 days of discharge is associated with reduced suicide risk
basis: Internal consistency check: §11 ('Ensure follow-up within 7 days… associated with reduced suicide risk and greater medication adherence') carries no hazard ratio. If an HR is wanted, it must be re-sourced (e.g., to a named cohort such as Che et al. 2023) rather than attributed to §11.

quote: MBC can improve remission rates by up to 75% compared to usual care.
problem: The sentence has no interpretable referent — 75% of what, relative or absolute, from what baseline — so it cannot be used, taught, or checked; it is most plausibly a garbling of the landmark MBC trial in which remission was ~74% with measurement-based care vs ~29% with usual care. As written a learner either repeats a meaningless statistic or reads it as 'remission improves to 75%', neither of which the literature says.
replacement: In the largest MBC trial in depression, remission was 74% with measurement-based care vs. 29% with usual care (Guo et al. 2015, Am J Psychiatry).
basis: Guo T et al., Am J Psychiatry 2015 (measurement-based care RCT in major depression: remission 73.8% vs 28.8%). Would be settled by confirming which source the 75% was extracted from.

quote: a **low-dose high-potency antipsychotic** (e.g., low-dose haloperidol) is the usual agent for agitation from delirium, targeting distressing psychosis/agitation that threatens safety — always at the **lowest effective dose**, with an **ECG/QTc** consideration and a plan to taper [3].
problem: The facilitator answer carries the QTc caveat but omits the other standard pre-antipsychotic check in a 74-year-old with 'mild memory problems': parkinsonism / possible dementia with Lewy bodies, where high-potency D2 blockade can cause severe neuroleptic sensitivity (profound rigidity, worsened confusion, NMS-like reactions). Teaching 'elderly agitated delirium → low-dose haloperidol' without that screen is exactly how DLB patients get hurt on a real unit.
replacement: a **low-dose high-potency antipsychotic** (e.g., low-dose haloperidol) is the usual agent for agitation from delirium, targeting distressing psychosis/agitation that threatens safety — always at the **lowest effective dose**, with an **ECG/QTc** consideration, a plan to taper, and a quick check for parkinsonism or suspected Lewy body dementia first, where antipsychotic sensitivity can be severe and haloperidol should be avoided [3].
basis: NICE delirium guidance (CG103) advises using antipsychotics with caution or not at all in Parkinson's disease and dementia with Lewy bodies; standard geriatric-psychiatry teaching on neuroleptic sensitivity in DLB.
